move: Concedes a circularity between freedom and self-legislation of the will, and proposes escaping it by distinguishing two standpoints from which we regard ourselves rather than by proving freedom.
Argues that freedom is the third cognition making the moral law's synthetic proposition possible, and concludes that freedom must be presupposed as a property of the will of all rational beings.

Affirms that every being that cannot act except under the idea of freedom is thereby really free in a practical respect, extending freedom a priori to all rational beings rather than deriving it from experience.
Holds that intentional choice presupposes a free causality expressed in character, and defends freedom against the mechanism of nature by appeal to the ideality of time.
Grants freedom objective reality only 'in a practical point of view' as the ground of a supersensible natural order given by the moral law, without asserting it theoretically.

Explicitly brackets the issue, noting the argument applies equally to a predetermined and an indeterminate universe, while adding that belief in free acts would raise their frequency if they are possible.
Rebuts the reductio that free will implies wild physical randomness by redefining it as the claim that among alternatives which genuinely tempt the will, more than one is really possible.
Claims freedom is the one speculative idea whose possibility we know a priori because it is the condition of the moral law, unlike God and immortality which are merely assumed.
Addresses political and social liberty — pursuing one's own good in one's own way free of coercion — rather than taking any position on metaphysical freedom of the will.
Reframes the issue as whether will operates causally at all, hypothesizing will to power as the single causality behind all force rather than affirming or denying freedom of the will.

Explains the belief in freedom as consciousness of one's actions combined with ignorance of their determining causes, identifying mental decision with a bodily appetite determined by the laws of motion.
Uses cases of the infant, angry child, drunkard, and delirious man to show that the felt 'free decision of the mind' accompanies impulses the agent cannot restrain.
